title: Add a REST read API for the patient record (patientrecord endpoint)
body:
## Purpose

Exposes QueryStore's authorized patient-record reads for external consumers, including
med-agent-hub, and supplies the shared **context-slice read contract** so every AI consumer uses
one context-selection implementation rather than drifting copies.

## What is here

- `GET /ws/rest/v1/querystore/patientrecord`: paged full chart with `snapshotId`, strong ETag,
  `304` revalidation, and clinical/administrative date semantics
  (`clinicalDate`, `dateKind`, `lastModified`); plus ranked top-K reads.
- **ADR Decision 17** - `getContextSlice(patient, question, {types, temporal})` and REST
  `mode=context`: tier-tagged `mandatory | recency_anchor | typed | similarity | panel`
  selection implemented at the data owner.
- **ADR Decision 18** - opt-in `interpret=true` plus server-side panel expansion and stopword
  preprocessing, eliminating measured interpretation drift between consumers.
- Reviewed read-safety follow-up:
  - bounds ranked result windows using OpenMRS's configured REST maximum;
  - prevents page arithmetic overflow;
  - reports `chartTruncated` only when a backend proves it omitted records;
  - makes panel expansion idempotent.

## Tests

`mvn -q -B clean install` passed at `e2cb359` with no test failures. Coverage includes
fixture-driven context-policy behavior, direct typed/temporal/interpreter tests, idempotent panel
preprocessing, controller `interpret=true` plumbing, bounded ranked windows, and overflow-safe
paging.

## Companion dependency

[ChartSearchAI #90](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/pull/90) consumes the
new `ContextSlice` API. It must not duplicate these classes: after this PR merges, the upstream
snapshot build must publish `querystore-api:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT`; then #90 will be re-cut from current
upstream and its Java matrix and product proof rerun against that published artifact.

title: Add the verify skill: ground a runtime claim in the running system
body:
The `verify` skill has been in use as a local install and committed nowhere. This puts it here, unchanged from the installed copy, so the set is installable from this repo rather than from whatever a given machine happens to have. `pr-harden` (#69) routes its standalone verifier through it, which is what surfaced the gap.

## What it pins

When a claim is about runtime behaviour — a deployed service, a database, an external API — the answer comes from that running thing. `curl` the endpoint and paste the bytes; drive the UI and capture the screenshot; SQL the live database; tail the log while triggering the behaviour. Reading code that *should* behave that way is not verification, a passing test is not production behaviour, and asking the user to check in their browser is a last resort rather than a first one.

It fixes the report shape too — what was run, what came back, what it was compared against, the verdict in one sentence — and requires the *absence* of verification to be said outright ("I could not verify because X") rather than papered over with code reasoning.

## One defect, left in deliberately

Draft because of this rather than because of the discipline. The **Per-project gates** section names a gate for this repo and chartsearchai:

> run the 10-query × 4-patient rubric (`/tmp/qs_fire_queries.sh` + `/tmp/qs_multi_patient_eval.py`)

Neither file exists. They are gone from `/tmp`, as `/tmp` files are, and they are in neither repo — so the section instructs a reader to run a gate that cannot be run, which is a worse failure than naming no gate at all. It is also exactly what the skill's own anti-patterns warn about: *reporting an endpoint you didn't verify exists*.

I left it as committed rather than editing it on the way in, because the fix is a decision rather than a typo — either those scripts get recovered and committed into this repo (`docs/` or a `scripts/` directory, referenced by a repo-relative path), or the gate reference is removed and the section says only "run the gate the project's CLAUDE.md or ADRs name". The second is a one-line change; the first is worth doing if the rubric is still the gate you want for retrieval and prompt changes.

Everything else in the file is project-neutral and needs no porting work — unlike #69, whose bodies still carry chartsearchai identifiers.

title: Add resolve-ticket and pr-harden: clean-context review rounds from a ticket to a mergeable PR
body:
Draft on purpose. The design is what I want read; the port is not finished and nothing has executed yet.

## What it is

`pr-harden` is a loop over an open PR. Each round: a fresh subagent reviews the pushed head through `pr-review`, a second fresh subagent implements every finding it agrees with and declines the rest on the record, the build is proved green, a verifier deploys to a real standalone where runtime behaviour is at stake, and one commit is pushed. It repeats until a review round reports **zero blocking findings**, then marks the PR ready.

`resolve-ticket` is the entry point — a GitHub issue or JIRA URL in, a ready-for-review PR out, unattended. Read the ticket with its comments, plan, refute the plan before any code exists, failing test first, implement, green, `harden` once with context, draft PR, then invoke `pr-harden` instead of handing back.

`pr-harden-gate.sh` is a Stop hook, shipped beside the skill the way `harden` 0.9.0 does it. It refuses to end the turn while a run is in flight or its last review found something blocking, and fails open on every ambiguity — no state file, malformed JSON, no `jq`, unrecognised phase, stale entry. Without it the convergence rules are prose, which is the state that lets them get skipped.

Three properties are load-bearing:

- **Every reviewer is a new subagent, never a fork.** It has never seen the code being argued for. This is the whole point; a fork inherits the transcript and defeats it.
- **The blocking count comes from the reviewer, never the fixer.** The agent being judged does not own the exit condition. A fixer that thinks a blocker is wrong declines it, and a declined blocker ends the run as *did not converge* rather than as success.
- **Only the declined ledger crosses rounds.** What was *fixed* is never shown to the next reviewer, so an insufficient fix is free to be re-raised on its own initiative, while a settled dispute does not recur. Without the ledger the loop cannot converge on a disputed finding; with the applied list too, the reviewer treats fixed areas as closed — which is exactly the suppression `harden`'s "re-derive the merged result from scratch" warns about.

## Why it is a draft — untested, and deliberately not yet module-neutral

No round has executed. That is the blocker.

The bodies are also not module-neutral: this repo is where the skills are committed, they install into `~/.claude/skills/` and run in **every** repo from there, so module-specific content is wrong wherever the skill runs outside the module it was written against. That is **deliberately deferred** until after a first real run in `openmrs-module-chartsearchai`, for a reason rather than for convenience: the chartsearchai identifiers below are the refutation gate's worked examples, and until a run shows whether that gate catches anything, generalising them would mean rewriting them twice. The exposure while deferred is bounded — a run in this repo would get examples pointing at another module's code — so do not invoke these here yet.

What carries that content today:

1. **Every `CLAUDE.md` example is from that module.** The refutation gate names a uniform ATC veto, longest-alias re-ranking, `rxcui`, `hasAllergyToken`; the anti-patterns name `buildPrefixedText`, `substanceKey`, `findImpliedByDrugName`, `groundedForWire`. None of those exist here, so a refuter told to look for them looks for the wrong things — worse than no examples at all. Each repo's own `CLAUDE.md` should supply them.
2. **The PR title voice is that module's.** Step 8 prescribes `type(scope): lowercase behaviour-after-fix` with an example; this repo's titles are plain sentence case (`Add a REST read API for the patient record`). The skill does say to read `gh pr list` and match, but the prescription fights it.
3. **The branch shape is that module's** — `fix/<issue>-<slug>` rather than what is used here.
4. **The verifier's environment specifics are that module's** (llama-server, its standalone, its scorer). The root-`mvn -o clean install` rationale probably does transfer, since the api + omod shape is the same, but the measurement behind it was taken there.
The verifier used to delegate to a `verify` skill, which made a load-bearing step depend on which skills a machine happened to have installed. It now carries the deploy procedure itself and depends on no other skill: config.xml for the module id and version, `$OPENMRS_STANDALONE_HOME` or the directory holding `openmrs-standalone.jar` rather than a hardcoded path, the port read from `openmrs-runtime.properties`, the second `.omod` of one module removed because it is a startup failure rather than a warning, the restart without which nothing is picked up, the timestamp check that catches verifying against stale bytes, and reading a saved value back out rather than trusting the screen.

Separately, while checking that: the installed set and the committed set here have drifted in both directions. `verify` (#70) and `measure-first` are installed but committed nowhere, and the installed `harden` is **0.8.0** against **0.9.0** here — so the machine running these is on the older copy of the very skill whose 0.9.0 change was to ship its hook alongside it.

## What has and has not run

**The front half has run for real**, against `openmrs-module-chartsearchai#285` in `--plan-only`: ticket resolution, the repo guard, the state entry and gate, the plan, and the refutation gate twice. It found **six defects in these skills, three of them blocking**, all fixed on this branch:

- The gate could not tell a run **waiting on a background subagent** from a run that quit. Every phase here delegates — the refutation gate, and each round's reviewer, fixer and verifier — so as first committed the loop could not have run unattended for a single round. Fixed with `awaiting` (0.1.3).
- A **partial mode had no terminus**: `--plan-only` stops at Step 3, a condition the gate can never clear, so the first run ended by taking the labelled override — the wrong instrument, since an override taken every time records nothing. Fixed (0.2.3), along with the `building` message naming phases the mode excludes.
- Step 3 and the autonomy contract **disagreed** about a second blocking objection: "bring it to the user" versus "abort only on ticket meaning". Neither anticipated a second objection that *settles* the question, which is what happened. Now three explicit outcomes, discriminated by whether the objection's citation determines the answer (0.2.4).
- Non-blocking: Step 2's `Explore` delegation was net-negative for narrow known-target lookups; `mode` was recorded but unread; the await mechanism needed writing on the skill side, not just reading on the hook side.

The refutation gate was the strongest component: three passes, two of the orchestrator's positions reversed, and four false justifications killed before any code existed — one of them on its way into a PR body.

**Not yet run:** Steps 4–9 (branch, failing test, implement, root install, `harden`, draft PR) and the entire loop — reviewer, fixer, verifier, commit, push, mark ready. The `awaiting` fix is verified in situ, but against one delegation shape; a round has three.

Nothing in `.claude/` executes from a PR branch — skills load from an installed or checked-out tree — so merging is what makes it available to install.

title: pr-harden 0.2.1 and resolve-ticket 0.3.1: snapshot the worktree before delegating
body:
The fourteenth defect the two real runs of this pipeline have found in it, and the only one the skills themselves **cause**.

Every reviewer, fixer and verifier brief tells the agent to mutate production code, run it, and restore it. That instruction is right — it is the strongest evidence available, and it produced most of the genuine findings in both runs. But nothing snapshotted the worktree, so the instruction had no counterpart.

**Measured.** A confirming agent died mid-response having changed `DrugReference.strictlyContains` from `start <= other.start && end >= other.end` to `start <= other.start`. The mutation was still in the tree when the notification arrived. It compiled, it read plausibly, most tests passed, and the agent never got to report — so nothing said it had happened. It would have gone into the round's commit, where that predicate silences overdose warnings. It was caught on a hunch about how the agent died, not by a rule.

Death is not the only path: an agent that forgets to restore looks identical from the orchestrator's seat.

**The rule.** Hash `git diff` before every delegation; compare after any terminal outcome — returned, failed, stalled, killed; restore from the snapshot on a mismatch and treat the residue as the agent's, never as a finding. It lives beside the clear-the-await rule because both fire on the same event. Briefs now also tell agents to restore **before** reporting, since a mutation restored late is one that ships if the agent dies mid-sentence — the eleven agents briefed that way afterwards all restored cleanly, verified by hash rather than trusted.

No behaviour change to the Stop hook.

title: skills: close the four silent edit-loss paths, and make correcting a claim mean finding every home of it
body:
Found by running `resolve-ticket` end to end on [chartsearchai#290](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/issues/290) → [PR #291](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/pull/291): 19 commits, 17 harden cycles, 3 review rounds, converged with zero blocking findings and a runtime verifier pass.

Every defect here is one the run hit, and every one was **silent** — nothing errored, the build stayed green, the tests passed:

| defect | how it surfaced |
|---|---|
| a reviewer's `restore` reverted a concurrent edit | a later test failed for a reason that made no sense |
| `str.replace` matched nothing and reported success | an agent found the claim five cycles later |
| a replacement slice deleted a neighbouring test method | counting test names |
| a correction reached 5 homes of 6 | the sixth was the PR description; a reviewer found it |

The last one is the recurring shape: on that run a correction reached one of seven homes, then five of six, then five of six again, and once **both halves of a single paragraph** disagreed after one half was fixed. So `pr-harden` gains a section saying a correction is not finished at the site you noticed it, naming the two homes a repo-wide grep never reaches — the project instruction file and the PR body.

Two smaller additions come from the same run: a finding may name the **PR description** and be blocking (round 2's only blocking finding was that), and a **verifier's observations can falsify the PR's prose** (the final verifier's live chip corrected the ADR's own benefit bullet).

Versions: `pr-harden` 0.2.1→0.3.0, `resolve-ticket` 0.3.1→0.4.0, `harden` 0.9.0→0.10.0. Installed copies under `~/.claude/skills` are synced.

title: skills: a standalone is disposable, so stop spending run time protecting it
body:
Three skills told their agents to protect the local OpenMRS standalone. The owner's instruction (2026-08-27) is that every standalone on these machines is a **throwaway demo instance, and so is its data** — so that protection buys nothing and costs run time.

Measured on the #315 run: the `pr-harden` verifier spent effort attributing pids, checking which ports were free, and preparing to report `unrepairable` rather than take the only standalone on the machine.

## Changed

| skill | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `pr-harden` §6 step 4 | never restart a server that was already running; report `unrepairable` if every candidate is in use | take it — "in use" is not a blocker |
| `pr-harden` repair bounds | prefer a reversible repair; report rather than perform an irreversible one | irreversibility is fine on a disposable instance |
| `resolve-ticket` §1 pre-flight | enumerate standalones, check listeners, a port you cannot attribute blocks | don't check the port; only *no standalone on disk* blocks |
| `verify-frontend-change` §3 | "don't clobber a server the user is using" | take it |

**Added**, because it is the half that actually wastes time: *do no data housekeeping in either direction* — don't back up or guard a standalone's data, and don't delete demo data you created to restore the original state.

## Deliberately NOT changed

- **The environment/artifact line.** Irreversible repairs to the standalone are fine; repairing the **artifact under test** — redeploying an older omod, reverting the round's commit, flipping a GP to route around a failing path — is still forbidden. A module that throws on startup looks identical to a broken environment from outside, so that rule is about fail-open verification, not about disposability.
- **Global-property restoration**, now stated unconditionally. They are configuration rather than data: a left-behind override silently changes what every later step measures, which is how an A/B ends up comparing the wrong two prompts.

## History kept

Each superseded rule keeps one line saying it was wrong about this environment and what it cost. Those rules were written after real incidents (a run nearly killed what it took to be the user's session; a verifier ran core liquibase against a standalone's DB), so without that note the next person hitting a busy port re-derives the same caution from scratch — which is how it got written the first time.

Versions bumped: `pr-harden` 0.11.0 → 0.12.0, `resolve-ticket` 0.12.0 → 0.13.0, `verify-frontend-change` 0.1.0 → 0.2.0.

title: skills: vendor verify and measure-first, which existed only on one machine
body:
`verify` and `measure-first` were hand-authored skills living in `~/.claude/skills` and nowhere else — unversioned, unbacked-up, and invisible to anyone else using this toolkit. Added at their current `0.1.0`, **unmodified**.

## Why now

Nothing is broken today: I grepped, and no skill in this repo references either of them. They are standalone guardrails rather than pipeline dependencies like `pr-review` is to `pr-harden`.

The risk being closed is that `~/.claude/skills` was a **partial mirror** of this directory — with exactly these two extra. A clean re-sync from `main` deletes them silently, and you find out when a skill you expected does not fire. Surfaced while preparing #73, which edits three skills here and made the divergence visible.

## What they are

| skill | lines | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `verify` | 60 | Guardrail: a claim about runtime behaviour must be answered by running the real system, not by reading code. Bans "all tests pass" without the count from the actual run. |
| `measure-first` | 72 | Forces a baseline + threshold gate before any change motivated by performance or quality rather than a known bug. |

## The one judgment call

Both are **generic**, not OpenMRS-specific, which is an odd fit for a module repo. I am adding them anyway because `harden`, `skill-retro` and `ticket-pool` are equally generic and already live here — this repo is already the de-facto home for the whole toolkit. Whether that toolkit should move somewhere neutral is a bigger question and is deliberately not proposed here.

Separate from #73 on purpose: that one changes behaviour and has trade-offs to weigh; this one is a straight vendoring with no judgment in it, and bundling them would mean neither got read properly.

title: A drug order that lapsed by its duration renders no end marker, so a text consumer cannot tell it from a live prescription
body:
`DrugOrderRecordSerializer` renders a drug order's end into the record text in two shapes and only two — `. Stopped: <date>` for `getDateStopped()` and `. Action: DISCONTINUE` for the action. It renders **nothing** for `auto_expire_date`.

So a prescription that simply ran out its duration reaches every text consumer byte-shaped exactly like one still being taken. The order is not active — `OrderService.getActiveOrders` excludes it — but nothing in the indexed text says so, and there is no field a consumer could read to find out.

## Measured

By running the real serializer rather than reading it. Pinned downstream by `QuerystoreOrderTextMarkerTest.anAutoExpireDateAloneIsNotVisibleInTheRenderedText` in `openmrs-module-chartsearchai`, which asserts the absence so a change here is noticed.

## Why this is being raised now

`chartsearchai` hit it twice and worked around it rather than fixing it here.

- [#316](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/issues/316) tried to teach an LLM prompt to tell ended orders from live ones. It cannot be done from the text: asked to sort records into two classes, the model puts the auto-expired one in the only class its text fits and then says so in a clinical answer. Reverted; recorded as ADR Decision 45.
- [#317](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/issues/317) worked around it by making chart assembly read `OrderService` directly and append its own `. Order status: in force` / `. Order status: not in force` field to each record. That is a second source of truth for something the record text could carry itself, and it cost `chartsearchai` a new `OrderService` dependency on its always-on path plus the `Get Orders` privilege.

There is a residue that traces straight back here. In [#321](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/pull/321), on a chart carrying several records of one drug where some have `. Stopped: <date>` and the auto-expired one has no date at all, the model asked *"has this drug been stopped?"* supplies the missing date by re-labelling that record's **order** date as a stop date, 3/3. Five prompt wordings failed to remove it. The plausible mechanism is that the record is the only one of its neighbours without the field they all carry — which would make it a symptom of this issue rather than of the prompt. **Not measured**, and it would need to be before anyone claims fixing this removes it.

## The design question, which is not "just render it"

`auto_expire_date` can be in the **future** — it is a scheduled expiry, not a record of an ending. Rendering it unconditionally as an end marker would assert that a live prescription has stopped, which is worse than the current silence. A faithful rendering has to distinguish the two, e.g. an expiry that has passed rendered as an ending and one still ahead rendered as a scheduled end, or not at all.

That is the substance of the change and why it is filed as a question rather than a patch.

## What would follow downstream if this is fixed

- `chartsearchai`'s `DrugReferenceInjector.describesEndedOrder` would cover auto-expiry for free, where today it covers only the two markers above.
- `QuerystoreOrderTextMarkerTest.anAutoExpireDateAloneIsNotVisibleInTheRenderedText`'s expectation flips — it is asserting today's behaviour, so it is the first thing that should go red.
- `chartsearchai`'s own structural mark (#317) would become redundant for this shape, though not for the others it covers (a failed order read, a record whose order cannot be attributed to the patient, an order core cannot evaluate).

## Caveat

This is a change to shared infrastructure: it alters the indexed text of every drug-order record for every query and every consumer, and it moves the bytes of any KV-cache prefix built over them. ADR Decision 46 in `chartsearchai` records it as needing its own plan and a full re-run of that module's regression gates, which is why the workaround was taken there instead of a change here.

title: ticket-pool 0.14.5: a ticket named by URL no longer builds a worktree path javac cannot compile in
body:
## The defect

`resolve_named` returned any non-digit token verbatim as a JIRA key. So `pool-run --work https://github.com/o/r/issues/238` made the whole URL the ticket's **identity** — and that identity reaches four things, not one: the worktree path, the ledger key, the lease file and the log stem.

The path is where it failed loudly. `worktree_path` interpolated the URL, and `Path` then ate the slashes:

```
BEFORE: <worktrees>/openmrs-openmrs-module-querystore-https:/github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-querystore/issues/238
        leaf='238'  inside WORKTREES=False  contains ':'=True

AFTER:  <worktrees>/openmrs-openmrs-module-querystore-238
        leaf='openmrs-openmrs-module-querystore-238'  inside WORKTREES=True  contains ':'=False
```

So the tree was created **outside `WORKTREES`**, three components deep, and carrying a **colon**. javac splits its classpath on `:`, so nothing in that tree could compile its tests — maven built `target/classes` and then failed every test with `cannot find symbol` against the classes it had just written. Main compiled; only the test classpath was broken, which is what made it look like a source problem.

Measured on a real run, which lost three build cycles before anyone suspected the path. A colon-free symlink does not help — maven canonicalises it.

The quieter half is the ledger. `pool-run --status` on that machine still shows two rows keyed on URLs, one stuck at `running`, unrelated to the `#238` and `#296` rows those tickets would otherwise have.

## The fix, at the root rather than at the path

- **`ticket_id()`** — one normaliser: GitHub issue/PR URL → number, JIRA browse URL → key, `#238` → `238`. Anything unrecognised comes back stripped but **not expanded**, because inventing an identifier for an unparseable token is how one ticket becomes two directories.
- **`ticket_repo()`** — only a URL says which repository owns it, so it is matched against the slug instead of tried against every repo. That is the difference between *"this repo does not own it"* and *"no repo does"*.
- **`worktree_path()`** — normalises **then** sanitises to a single `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` component. Both halves earn their place: normalising makes a URL and its number the same tree rather than two; sanitising keeps a token nobody thought of from reaching the filesystem at all. `/` silently nests and `..` walks out of `WORKTREES`, so the colon was never the only hazard.
- **`resolve_named`, `cmd_work`, `cmd_claim`, `release_claim`** all carry the identifier onward. `cmd_work` is the one that actually caused this: it called `resolve_named` (which reduced the token) and then passed the **raw** token to `work_in_session`, un-reducing it. `--release` had to move with `--claim`, or it would no longer find the lease `--claim` had just written.

**Every other token shape behaves exactly as before** — `238`, `#238`, `o/r#238` and a bare JIRA key produce the same directories and keys they did.

## How it is verified

`test_ticket_identity`, written failing first. It covers the reduction, the repo routing, and the path guarantees — including that a URL and its number resolve to **one** worktree, and that two tickets still get two. Adversarial inputs (`weird/../thing`, `a:b`) are asserted to stay inside `WORKTREES` as a single safe component.

The identifier itself is asserted on `ticket_id` rather than through `resolve_named`: that function's digit branch verifies the issue with a real `gh issue view`, so asserting the number there would be asserting that the machine can reach GitHub, which is not what is under test. Stated because the first draft of the test did exactly that and failed for the wrong reason.

`python3 .claude/pipeline/pool-test.py`: **255 passed, 0 failed** — run in a fresh clone of this branch, not only on the machine the fix was written on.

## Scope

Driver and its test only, matching `ticket-pool 0.14.4`, which touched the same two files and likewise left the skill frontmatter alone.

Not included, and flagged rather than fixed silently:

- **The two polluted ledger rows** on the affected machine. They are owned by a `pool-run --work <url>` process that is still alive, so re-keying them would race a live writer. They can be migrated once it drains; this change stops new ones being created.
- **`clone-slots`** exists in `~/.claude/pipeline` on that machine but is absent from this repo. That may be deliberate; I have not added it.

title: pool-run: report what ENDED a session, instead of asserting the loop did not converge
body:
## What was wrong

The driver decides a run's outcome from **evidence** — a PR exists, and whether it is draft — deliberately not from the session's own closing prose. That is the right basis. But it cannot distinguish a loop that genuinely ran out of rounds from one whose session was killed before its closing steps ran, and the `draft` verdict asserted the first about both:

```python
"draft": f"PR #{...} left as a DRAFT — the loop did not converge",
```

## Measured

On `openmrs-module-chartsearchai#349` the review loop **had** converged — gate state `phase=reviewed blocking=0 round=1`, and the round-1 verifier had already confirmed the fix live against the ticket's own fixture patient. An API refusal (`stop_reason: "refusal"`, category `reasoning_extraction`) then ended the session before it could mark the PR ready or write its run record. `pool-run` reported *"the loop did not converge"*.

That is a false diagnosis rather than a thin one: it sends an operator looking for review findings that do not exist, and it hid the fact that the work was finished. The missing run record — for which the driver wrote a capture in its place — has the same single cause.

## The change

- `Session.run()` carries `stop_reason` out of the final result record. Everything else in that record was already read; this field was dropped on the floor.
- The ledger records it as `ended_by`. Absent rather than null on a `--work` row, since that launcher reads no stream-json and has a human watching instead.
- `draft_cause()` names the cause where the session reported one, and otherwise says exactly what the line said before.

## Why `draft_cause` is its own function

Two reasons, both found reviewing the first commit rather than writing it.

It keys on **"not a normal end"**, never on the reasons that have been observed. Keying on `stop_reason == "refusal"` — the one value seen — reproduces this very defect for the next unknown reason. Only `end_turn` and `refusal` occur across the streams this was written against, and five streams establish nothing about what else the API may report.

And it is a function because nothing in the suite executes `work_ticket` — the single case that reaches it reads its **source text** (`pool-test.py`, `body.index("def work_ticket(")`), and there is no `gh` stub to drive `open_prs`. An inline branch there is a wording no test can pin, in the one line whose whole job is not misleading an operator. `common_claude_args` was extracted for the same reason.

## Testing

`python3 .claude/pipeline/pool-test.py`: **341 passed, 0 failed** (337 before this branch; all still green).

- `test_a_session_reports_what_ended_it` drives the real `Session.run()` over a stub `claude` emitting a result record with `stop_reason: "refusal"` — the same substitution the rest of the suite uses, and the real stream-parsing path. It fails on the parent commit with `stop_reason == None` while its two neighbouring assertions (`is_error`, `summary`) pass, so it pins this gap and not the surrounding behaviour.
- `test_a_draft_is_not_told_the_loop_ran_out_of_rounds` covers `draft_cause` over four shapes: a refusal, an abnormal reason nobody has seen yet, a normal `end_turn`, and a session that reported nothing. The second is the widening's own guard — narrowing the key back to one value reddens it.

## Deliberately not done

Whether a refusal should spend the second attempt is a separate decision, and this PR is reporting-only. On #349 a blind retry would have redone four hours of finished work. Resuming the session — whose transcript survives, and for which `--resume` machinery already exists for pauses — is the cheaper candidate, but it changes recovery behaviour and wants its own decision.

Nothing runs `pool-test.py` in CI (no workflow references `.claude`), so this suite only executes when someone types it. Out of scope here; worth its own change.

title: Step 9 runs the review loop on a loaded orchestrator, costing 11.9% of pipeline input tokens
body:
`resolve-ticket` Step 9 invokes `pr-harden` in the same session, so the orchestrator drives the whole
review loop while still carrying Steps 1–8. Measured over 20 tickets / 21 sessions of the pipeline
(10,135,653,777 input tokens), that costs **1,203,742,395 tokens — 11.9% of all input**, and every
ticket pays it.

This is not primarily a cost issue. `pr-harden`'s design premise is review by agents who never watched
the code being written; the orchestrator driving that loop is the one participant for which the premise
is false, and it is also where the loop's correctness state lives — the declined-findings ledger and
`reviewed_shas`, which is what stops a round re-reviewing a sha already reviewed.

## Measurement

At the moment `pr-harden` is invoked the orchestrator is already at **500,867** tokens (#238) and
**644,302** (#339), and it then takes 486 and 337 further turns on top of that. Peaks reached:

| ticket | orchestrator peak | of the 1M context window |
|---|---|---|
| #339 | 971,327 | 97% |
| #238 | 907,247 | 91% |
| #330 | 813,683 | 81% |
| #266 | 806,675 | 81% |

No run shows a drop to a plausible post-compaction level, so nothing is managing that headroom.

**To reproduce.** For each `~/.claude/projects/*pipeline-worktrees*/` orchestrator `.jsonl` plus its
`<session-uuid>/subagents/*.jsonl`, per-turn context is
`usage.cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens` on assistant messages.
Boundary = the first `Skill{skill:"pr-harden"}` tool call. Saving = (context **at** the boundary −
fresh-session floor) × post-boundary orchestrator turns. Note two traps: one directory (#346) holds
two sessions of one ticket while the ledger records `attempts: 1`, and the fresh-floor constant is
post-`CLAUDE.md`-cut, so applying today's floor to older boundaries slightly over-credits the change.

An independent re-derivation reproduced the denominator to 0.009% and the gross saving to 0.85%.

## Two designs, both refuted

**A — a `--to-pr` terminus on `resolve-ticket` plus a second driver-launched session.** Five blocking
objections. The handover state entry gates nothing, because an entry whose `owner` pid is dead allows
exactly as hard as no entry (`pr-harden-gate.sh`, pinned in `pr-harden/gate-test.sh`). The new gate
phase would allow *unconditionally*, since the phase switch ends `*) allow` — and `gate-state` will not
write one anyway (`PHASES` is a closed tuple used as argparse `choices`). And it changed the driver
path while 16 of 18 ledger rows are `launched_by: "work"`, interactive sessions the driver never
touches — including both near-ceiling runs the case rested on.

**B — the parent backgrounds `claude -p '/pr-harden <n>'` and collects it in-turn.** Seven blocking
objections. Two are structural: `unattended_marker` has exactly one call site, in the headless worker,
so on an interactive ticket the child would run as a `claude -p` with no termination contract — the
death recorded for #297 and #310; and a background task gets its own process group, so `killpg` from
the driver cannot reach it, leaving a child that survives a timeout or a pause still holding the
worktree and still pushing.

## What both have in common

Each design's central mechanism was that **an ownership stamp disarms a Stop gate**. That is what
killed A, and B then used it deliberately as a feature. The underlying reason is that ownership is an
upward `ps -o ppid=` walk, identical in both gates, both keyed on `pwd -P` — so it is asymmetric by
construction, and the two gates give opposite answers about the same parent/child pair. And "not ours"
is an *exit*, not a relaxation: `allow()` is `exit 0` and the ownership rung precedes every other
check, so "the parent may yield" and "the parent is ungated" are the same sentence.

## The question underneath

**May one checkout carry more than one contract at a time?** Everything above follows from "one
checkout, one entry, one owner". A third design that routes around that assumption will meet it again;
answering it deliberately is the work.

## Verified vs estimated

Verified against source or transcripts: every token figure, both peaks, the `*) allow` case, the
`gate-state` phase rejection, the single `unattended_marker` call site, the `launched_by` split, and
the process-group behaviour. Estimated: dollar figures — the sessions record `totalCostUSD` summing to
$4,570.60, so prefer that to any list-price computation.

Separately and independently: nothing probes whether a standalone's ports are actually held before a
slot is handed over — `standalone_ports()` reads the properties file and only when `workers > 1`. That
is worth its own issue.

title: Nothing checks whether a standalone's ports are already held before a slot is handed to a run
body:
`standalone_ports()` (`.claude/pipeline/pool-run:442`) reads `tomcatport` and `dbport` out of a
standalone's `openmrs-runtime.properties`. It is a **configuration** read, and it is the only thing
the driver knows about ports. Two call sites: `Slot.__init__` (`:515`), which puts them in the run's
environment, and the preflight (`:643`), which reports two standalones *configured* to bind the same
port — and only when `parallel.max_workers > 1`.

**Nothing ever asks whether a port is currently held.** `grep -cE 'connect_ex|socket\(|bind\(|LISTEN|lsof|netstat|is_port'` over `pool-run` returns 0, and no skill uses `lsof` or `netstat` either. So the
preflight catches config-vs-config collisions and never config-vs-reality.

## Why that gap has something to fall into

The driver's only stop is `os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), ...)` (`:1737`, `:1739`, `:3049`) against
the claude session's process group. Anything a run detaches — a backgrounded server, a launcher that
forks and exits — leaves that group and is unreachable. So a killed, timed-out or paused ticket can
leave its standalone running.

Measured on the development machine, 2026-09-01: an `openmrs-standalone.jar` with its tomcat and
mariadbd, PPID 1, ~10 h old, **holding :8081 and :3316**, in a process group that no live `claude`
process owns (checked against the pgid of every running one). Its home is
`~/Downloads/referenceapplication-standalone-3.7.1`, which is **slot 1's assigned standalone in
`pool.json`**. A `llama-server` and an 89-day-old `zsh` from a `~/.claude/shell-snapshots/` script were
orphaned the same way.

## Why the run cannot recover on its own

`pr-harden` forbids a verifier taking a server it did not start, and that rule is deliberate and
measured — the near-miss it was written for involved an attributable `java -jar openmrs-standalone`,
which is why attribution alone was found insufficient. The rule is correct. It also means a run handed
an occupied slot can neither use the port nor clear it, so the failure surfaces at standalone startup
as something that looks unrelated, and nothing in the pipeline will ever tidy it up.

## Severity: latent, not currently biting

Slots 2–5 (`pool-slots/standalone-808{2,3,4,5}`) have nothing running. The one occupied slot may be a
deliberate permanent test rig rather than a leak — `ps` cannot tell those apart, which is itself part
of the problem.

## Shape of a fix

A liveness probe at claim time, beside the existing config check, would turn a confusing startup
failure into a clear refusal naming the port and the holding pid. Whether the driver should then skip
the slot, wait, or abort is a policy question, not an obvious default. `standalone_ports()` already
returns exactly the two ports that would need probing, so the missing piece is small.

Related: #78 (the Stop-gate ownership model, where the `killpg` reach problem is item 8 of the same
analysis).

title: A repository that cannot be fetched erases a paused ticket's resume pointers
body:
`pool-run --resume` against a repository whose `git fetch` fails rewrites every **paused** ticket on
that repository to `checkout-blocked`, stripping the two fields a resume needs. A ledger-only pause —
which the driver's own docstring calls "the durable half" — is then unrecoverable, because nothing
can find it as paused any more.

The path is `prepare_bases` (`.claude/pipeline/pool-run`), which applies `nothing_ran` to every job
queued against a repository it could not prepare. `nothing_ran` strips `RUN_FIELDS`, and
`session_id` and `worktree` are both in that set.

### Measured

Through the production functions, against an isolated ledger (`prepare_bases`, `nothing_ran`,
`write_ledger`, `paused_from_ledger` — no reimplementation of any of them):

```
BEFORE : {"status": "paused", "session_id": "sess-abc123", "worktree": ".../wt/o-r-266"}
discoverable as paused BEFORE: ['o/r#266']
  x o/r: could not fetch origin: fatal: not a git repository ...
    Nothing was touched. The repository could not be fetched or its default branch could not be
    resolved on origin (the line above says which); fix that, then re-run.
AFTER  : {"status": "checkout-blocked", "session_id": null, "worktree": null}
discoverable as paused AFTER : []
```

`SUSPENDED` is `{'paused'}`, so once the status is `checkout-blocked` the row is invisible to
`paused_from_ledger`, and `--resume` reports there is nothing paused.

### Why it matters

* **`--resume` is exactly when the fetch fails.** A pause is an invitation to come back much later;
  coming back on a different network, or to a moved clone, is the ordinary case. The one flow whose
  whole purpose is to re-enter a suspended session is the flow that destroys the pointers into it.
* **The plan file is not a general mitigation.** A pause named by `paused.json` survives, because the
  plan carries the session and worktree itself. A pause the plan never recorded does not — and
  `paused_from_ledger`'s docstring is explicit that this is a real state and that the ledger is what
  it relies on: "A driver that dies in that gap — or at any point after it — leaves a paused ticket
  with no plan naming it … So the plan is treated as what it is, an extra … and the ledger as the
  durable half."
* **It contradicts what the driver says while doing it.** The remedy line printed at that moment
  reads "Nothing was touched." `SKILL.md`'s outcomes table says `checkout-blocked` means "so nothing
  was touched", and "It costs no attempt: nothing ran." All three are true of the *worktree* and
  false of the *ledger row*.

### Scope

Pre-existing, and not introduced by the notification work: the per-ticket `nothing_ran` write dates
from `1abe18b` (2026-08-27, ticket-pool 0.9.2). `736619e` moved the block into `prepare_bases`
unchanged. It surfaces now only because the operator gets a `repo-blocked` push that counts the
stalled tickets while saying nothing about the paused rows it has just rewritten.

### Direction, not a prescription

A ticket that is mid-attempt has no outcome to record — a blocked fetch is a statement about the
remote, not about that run. The narrow fix is for `prepare_bases` to leave a row alone when its
status is in `SUSPENDED`, and if the block is worth recording there at all, to record it as a flag
rather than as a status. Worth deciding at the same time: whether the `repo-blocked` escalation
should name the suspended tickets separately, since "3 tickets cannot start" reads differently when
one of them is a session waiting to be re-entered.

Whatever the shape, it wants a case in `pool-test.py` that pauses a ticket, blocks its repository,
and asserts the row is still resumable — the suite has the fixtures for both halves already
(`test_pause_now_suspends_and_resumes`, `test_the_ledger_is_the_durable_half_of_a_pause`).

title: Render a birthdate as the date it holds on servers east of UTC
body:
Fixes #81

On a JVM east of UTC a patient document stated a birthdate one day earlier than `person.birthdate`, in both the text (`Born …`) and the `birthdate` metadata. `DateFormatUtil.formatDate` converts every `Date` through a UTC instant. `birthdate` is a `DATE` column that Hibernate hands back as a `Timestamp` at local midnight, so that conversion moves it back a day wherever the zone's offset is positive.

**Change**
- `DateFormatUtil.formatCalendarDate` renders a date-only value in the JVM default zone, the zone JDBC reads and writes the column in. It goes through `getTime()` rather than `toInstant()`, which `java.sql.Date` throws on.
- `PatientRecordSerializer` uses it for `birthdate`. In core's schema snapshot, `person.birthdate` is the only `DATE` column a serializer formats. Every other formatted field is a `datetime` column and still renders in UTC, pending #59.
- The ADR's *Timestamp time-zone convention* open question now records that date-only columns are outside it.
- `DateFixtures.localMidnight` builds the local-midnight shape. The ADR-example test used a UTC-noon birthdate, which renders as the next day on a host at UTC+12 or beyond once birthdate is read in the host zone.

**Verification**
- New `PatientRecordSerializerTest` cases drive `serialize` with the zone pinned (Africa/Nairobi, Pacific/Kiritimati) and the birthdate built after pinning it: a local-midnight `Timestamp` and a `java.sql.Date`. On `main` they render `1962-09-20` / `2015-06-13` and throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, and they pass with the fix.
- The suite passes under `-Duser.timezone` = Pacific/Auckland, America/Los_Angeles and Pacific/Kiritimati. Before the fixture change, Auckland failed the ADR-example test with `Born 1982-07-15`.
- `mvn clean install` passes from the repository root under JDK 8.

title: A birthdate renders one day early on servers east of UTC: DateFormatUtil converts a date-only value through a UTC instant
body:
## Problem

On a JVM whose default time zone is east of UTC, a patient document states a birthdate one day earlier than the database holds, in the text and in the `birthdate` metadata. Observed on a RefApp 3.7.1 standalone whose JVM runs in `Africa/Nairobi` (UTC+3):

| Patient | `person.birthdate` | patient document text |
|---|---|---|
| `83f95445-d471-4e9c-b10e-a89b6632dbe8` | 1962-09-21 | `Patient: Helen Roberts. Female. Born 1962-09-20` |
| `de4b0d62-8a47-4c82-8220-1f0a87eafd46` | 2015-06-14 | `Patient: Mark Smith. Male. Born 2015-06-13` |

The text is as chartsearchai received it from querystore after a `POST /querystore/reindex` for each patient; querystore has no endpoint that returns a document. A clinician asking a chart question therefore reads the wrong date of birth, as a cited record.

## Root cause

`DateFormatUtil.formatDate` renders every `Date` through a UTC instant:

```java
return date.toInstant().atZone(UTC).toLocalDate().format(DATE_FORMAT);
```

`person.birthdate` is a `DATE` column, and core maps it as `type="java.util.Date"` (`Person.hbm.xml` in openmrs-api 2.9.0-SNAPSHOT, the version querystore builds against). Hibernate therefore hands the serializer a `java.sql.Timestamp` at local midnight (a `java.sql.Date` would throw, see below, and the live rig does not). 1962-09-21 00:00 in Nairobi is 1962-09-20 21:00 UTC, so the rendered date moves back one day whenever the JVM zone's offset is positive. A calendar date has no instant, and converting it through one changes it.

## Reproduced on main (6f15b1c) through the real serializer

A throwaway test calling `PatientRecordSerializer.serialize` with the birthdate in the shape Hibernate produces, `java.sql.Timestamp.valueOf("1962-09-21 00:00:00")`, run with `-DargLine=-Duser.timezone=<zone>`:

| JVM zone | metadata `birthdate` | text |
|---|---|---|
| `Africa/Nairobi` | 1962-09-20 | `… Born 1962-09-20` |
| `UTC` | 1962-09-21 | `… Born 1962-09-21` |
| `America/New_York` | 1962-09-21 | `… Born 1962-09-21` |

The existing `PatientRecordSerializerTest` stays green under `-Duser.timezone=Africa/Nairobi`. `DateFixtures.utcDate` builds every date at 12:00 UTC, deliberately so the suite is host-independent, and a midday-UTC instant formats to the same date in any zone. Real date-only values arrive at local midnight, a shape the fixture never produces, so no test can see this.

## Reach

`DateFormatUtil` is shared, so the same conversion renders `death_date`, condition onset and end, program enrolled and completed, order stop and auto-expire, obs `value_datetime`, dispense handed-over, and every document's record date. For those timestamps, which zone is right is #59's question. In practice a value with a daytime time moves only when its local time is earlier than the zone's offset (00:00–03:00 in Nairobi): Helen Roberts' program enrollment, stored at 09:16, renders correctly. `birthdate` is different. It is a `DATE` column with no time to convert, and it moves for every patient, as does any timestamp stored at midnight because it was entered as a date.

## Relation to #59

#59 tracks the time-zone convention for timestamps, and the ADR's open question itself separates date-only fields (`record_date`, `birthdate`) from timestamp fields. This is the date-only half, and it is a defect rather than a convention: a value stored without a time should render as the date it holds, whatever #59 settles for timestamps.

## Notes for a fix

- Render a date-only value in the zone it was materialized in (the JVM default zone JDBC used), not in UTC.
- `java.sql.Date.toInstant()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, and `formatDate` hits it in every zone (the same throwaway test, given `java.sql.Date.valueOf("1962-09-21")`). No field querystore formats arrives as one from core today: no core `hbm.xml` uses `type="date"`, and `Condition`, `MedicationDispense` and `PatientProgram` carry no `TemporalType`. A fix should still not route a date through `toInstant()` if it can ever receive one.
- A regression test needs the real shape, a local-midnight value under a JVM zone east of UTC, which `DateFixtures.utcDate` cannot express.

title: Sync: create-then-void/delete race leaves stale voided documents searchable (delete is not version-ordered like upsert)
body:
## Summary

A record that is **created and then voided/deleted in quick succession** can be left in the read store as a **stale, still-searchable document**, because the async sync pipeline's `delete` is not version-ordered the way `upsert` is. The delete can execute *before* the create's (slower) index write lands, so the delete no-ops and the subsequent upsert resurrects a document for a record that is actually voided/gone.

This is a `sync`-layer eventual-consistency defect. It is **not** in any serializer or in a specific `ResourceTypeProvider` — the disposition logic (`voided → delete`) is computed correctly. It affects **every** resource type; it was simply easy to trigger via `bill`/`billDiscount`/`billRefund` REST calls.

## Environment

- querystore `1.0.0-SNAPSHOT`, platform `2.9.0-SNAPSHOT`, **Lucene** backend
- Reference Application standalone `3.7.0-rc.2`
- Observed while verifying the billing → querystore integration (`billing-querystore` omod), but the racing machinery is entirely in querystore's `sync` package.

## Root cause

The write and delete halves of the pipeline are asymmetric with respect to the conditional-upsert-by-version invariant (ADR Decision 3):

- `BackendStore.upsert(doc)` **is** version-guarded — a write whose `last_modified` is older than the stored version is dropped (`BackendStore.java:51-56`; Lucene/MySQL/ES all honor it, e.g. ES `external_gte`). This makes **upsert-vs-upsert** monotonic per `resource_uuid`: freshest wins regardless of execution order.
- `BackendStore.delete(resourceType, resourceUuid)` **is unconditional** (`BackendStore.java:58`). The Lucene impl is a bare term delete with no version predicate:
  ```java
  // LuceneBackendStore.java:158-161
  public WriteResult delete(String resourceType, String resourceUuid) {
      ...
      writer.deleteDocuments(new Term(LuceneFieldNames.RESOURCE_UUID, resourceUuid));
  }
  ```
  There is no versioned tombstone. A delete carries no logical timestamp, so it cannot "win" against a concurrent-or-later upsert.

Now combine that with how tasks are scheduled:

1. `RecordProjector.project(...)` correctly routes a voided node to `toDelete` and a live node to `toIndex`, then hands the work to `AfterCommitDispatcher.dispatch(...)`.
2. `AfterCommitDispatcher.dispatch` registers an `afterCommit()` synchronization that does `executor.submit(guarded)` — one submission **per source transaction**.
3. `SyncExecutor` is a **multi-worker** `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(poolSize, ...)` (`SyncExecutor.java:66`) with **no per-`resource_uuid` ordering**.
4. `RecordIndexer.index(doc)` computes an **embedding first** (`embeddingProvider.embed(...)`) before writing — a comparatively slow step — while `RecordIndexer.delete(...)` is a fast term delete.

So for `create record R` (txn A commits → submit `upsert(R, v1)`) followed shortly by `void/delete record R` (txn B commits → submit `delete(R)`):

- the two tasks run on different pool threads, unordered;
- `delete(R)` finishes first (fast, and/or scheduled first) and removes nothing — the doc isn't written yet;
- `upsert(R, v1)` then completes the slow embed and writes the doc;
- the version guard does **not** save us: there is no newer *versioned* record to compare against (the delete left no tombstone), so v1 is written and **survives**.

Net: a voided/deleted record remains indexed and searchable.

### Why the ADR's self-healing argument doesn't cover this

`AfterCommitDispatcher.wrap(...)` documents (per ADR Decision 12) that a missed projection is "corrected by the next save or the bootstrap pass — neither overwrites the freshest document." That holds for a **lost upsert** (under-indexing, repaired by the next save). It does **not** hold for a **lost delete**: a voided/purged record is terminal — there is no "next save" — so the stale document persists until the reconciliation path (`GET /querystore/drift` + `POST /querystore/reindex`) is run. It is silent over-indexing, not self-healing.

## Reproduction (observed)

On the standalone above, with the billing types (any type works — see below):

**Fast path — race fires:**
1. `POST /billing/bill` (create) then, within ~1s, `DELETE /billing/bill/{uuid}` (void).
2. `GET /querystore/drift` → `billing_bill` shows `indexedCount = coreCount + 1`, `drift = -1`.
3. The voided bill is still returned by `POST /chartsearchai/search` for that patient (a clinician sees a cancelled bill).

Concrete run: created bill `0009-1`, voided its refund and then the bill back-to-back; final `drift` reported `billing_bill core=3 index=4` — the voided bill stayed. A `chartsearchai` query then listed it: `"Bill 0007-5: 300.00"` for a bill that was `voided=1` in the DB.

**Settled path — no race:**
1. `POST /billing/bill`; **poll `/querystore/drift` until the index reflects the create** (index write has landed).
2. `DELETE /billing/bill/{uuid}`.
3. `/querystore/drift` returns to `drift = 0` — the delete purges correctly every time.

The only variable is whether the create's async index write has landed before the delete is dispatched. This is the signature of a create-then-delete ordering race, not a logic error.

**Not billing-specific / not a serializer bug:**
- `SyncExecutor`, `AfterCommitDispatcher`, `RecordProjector`, `RecordIndexer`, `BackendStore.delete` are all type-agnostic.
- A SQL-forced `PAID` bill with **no** child voided and purged cleanly, ruling out entity state as the cause.
- The same rapid create→delete on `obs`/`condition`/etc. is expected to reproduce identically; only the ease of firing two quick REST writes differs.

## Impact

- **Correctness:** a voided/deleted clinical record can remain searchable in the read store until a reindex. For a clinician-facing chart search this is a trust/safety issue (surfacing a cancelled bill, a deleted obs, etc.).
- **Likelihood:** low at human interaction speed (seconds between create and void let the index settle). Higher under automated/bulk writers, scripted corrections, imports, or double-click/void-immediately UX.
- **Backend scope:** the asymmetry (versioned upsert, unversioned delete) is in the shared contract; Lucene confirmed, MySQL/ES have the same unconditional `delete`.

## Detection & workaround (today)

- Detect: `GET /querystore/drift` — a negative `drift` (index > core) flags exactly this class of stale extra.
- Repair: `POST /querystore/reindex {"patient":"<uuid>"}` (per patient) or `{"scope":"all"}` — delete + rebuild from non-voided core. Confirmed to clear the stale doc.

## Suggested fixes (for discussion)

1. **Versioned tombstone / conditional delete.** Give `delete` the same version semantics as `upsert`: a void/delete writes a tombstone carrying the source `last_modified`, and `upsert` refuses to resurrect over a `>=` tombstone (and `delete` refuses to remove a strictly-newer doc). This extends the existing conditional-by-version invariant to cover the terminal op and makes per-`resource_uuid` writes monotonic regardless of execution order. Preferred — it keeps the lock-free, unordered executor.
2. **Per-`resource_uuid` ordering.** Route all pipeline ops for a given `(resourceType, resource_uuid)` through a single ordered lane (hash the uuid to a fixed worker, or a per-key sequential executor) so submission order = execution order. Simpler to reason about; costs some parallelism and needs care with the embed step.
3. **Re-check liveness at write time.** Before the terminal `upsert`, re-verify the source record is still non-voided/extant. Weakest (still racy, adds a read), noted only for completeness.

## Pointers

- `api/.../sync/RecordProjector.java` — `project(...)` disposition + dispatch
- `api/.../sync/AfterCommitDispatcher.java` — `dispatch(...)` → `executor.submit(...)`
- `api/.../sync/SyncExecutor.java:66` — `newFixedThreadPool(poolSize, ...)`
- `api/.../sync/RecordIndexer.java` — `index(...)` (embed-then-upsert) vs `delete(...)`
- `api/.../backend/BackendStore.java:51-58` — versioned `upsert` vs unconditional `delete`
- `api/.../backend/lucene/LuceneBackendStore.java:158-161` — unconditional term delete

title: Expose patient records over REST with explicit completeness and date semantics
body:
First of three pull requests that replace #68, split as asked there. Each builds on the one before it and all three target main; #88 continues the stack with the retrieval changes moved out of #87, and the query-cache separator change is in #89.

**What this adds**

- `GET /ws/rest/v1/querystore/patientrecord`: the full chart by `patient`, or a ranked top-K by `patient` and `q` (or `q` alone). Every mode requires the `Get Patients` privilege, and each record is returned only if the caller holds its type's core read privilege (`Get Observations`, `Get Orders`, and so on); unknown modes and malformed typed parameters return 400.
- Paging honours the live `webservices.rest.maxResultsAbsolute` ceiling: an oversized `limit` is clamped, a ranked window past the ceiling returns 400, and `links` carry the effective page size.
- Completeness is explicit. `chartTruncated` comes only from the backend's own signal (an Elasticsearch size limit, failed shard, timeout or early termination; a MySQL per-table read failure; a Lucene per-index failure or an index the enumerator could not open). `projectionComplete` reports the deployment-wide bootstrap state, and a failed lazy projection for one patient, including one that projected only some of its records, is disclosed on the read rather than returned as an empty complete chart. The snapshot fingerprint and the ETag include both bits.
- Dates: each record carries `clinicalDate` and `dateKind` (`clinical_event`, `administrative`, `unknown`) beside the sort date; providers of custom record types declare `date_kind`.
- `Cache-Control: private, no-cache, must-revalidate` on every exit; the full chart carries an ETag.

**What the tests pin:** a handled backend failure is never reported as a complete empty chart; paging never links to a request the controller rejects; existing in-JVM `QueryStoreService` implementations keep working.

title: Skip records stored at their current version during a bootstrap top-up
body:
A restart's bootstrap top-up re-projected every record changed since the last checkpoint, most of which steady-state sync had already indexed at that version, while the type stayed `RUNNING` (6.4 minutes for 5,000 obs on the demo data). Raised in the review of openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai#587.

**What this changes**

- `BackendStore.findLastModified(resourceType, uuids)` returns each stored record's `last_modified`, implemented on Lucene, MySQL and Elasticsearch; the default reports none, so a custom backend keeps today's behaviour.
- A top-up page projects only records that are not stored or whose stored version differs from the scanned one, compared to the second (core stores audit dates to the second). A forced resync still re-projects everything.
- Sync wrote new records without `last_modified`, because the save event publishes before the save stamps `dateCreated`; the after-commit write now reads the version off the committed entity, so the backend's version guard applies to synced records too.

**Verified** with unit tests on each backend, `-Pintegration` against Elasticsearch and MySQL, and on a running stack: after a restart, a record written by bootstrap and one written by sync were both skipped. ADR: the backend SPI list and the bootstrap paragraph.

Based on `main`; independent of #85 to #87.

title: Delete Elasticsearch documents at their own version so a same-version rewrite applies
body:
## Problem

`POST /querystore/reindex {"patient"}` on the Elasticsearch backend returns 200 with `documentsIndexed: 0` whenever it runs within about a minute of the previous delete of that patient's documents, and the patient's chart is empty afterwards. The service logs nothing and counts every write as confirmed. On a live stack one reindex of a 320-record patient removed all 320 documents and wrote none, while the Elasticsearch `index_failed` counter rose by 320 per shard copy.

## Cause

Documents are written with `version_type=external_gte` and `version=last_modified`. Elasticsearch keeps a tombstone for a deleted document for `index.gc_deletes` (60 s by default) and rejects a versioned write at or below the tombstone's version. The store's deletes were unversioned (`delete_by_query`, bulk delete, single delete), which sets the tombstone one above the document's version. `reindexPatient` deletes the patient's documents and then rewrites the same records at the same `last_modified`, so every rewrite is a version conflict, and `countBulkSuccess` counted a 409 as a stale write skipped, that is, as success.

The same tombstone drops the rewrite after a patient-merge sweep and the re-projection of a record unvoided within a minute of being voided.

## Fix

Every Elasticsearch delete is now issued at the document's own external version (`bulkDeleteByPatient` reads ids and versions a page at a time and deletes each at that version; `bulkDelete` reads versions with `mget`; `delete` reads the version with `get`). The tombstone then carries the record's own timestamp: an equal-or-newer rewrite applies, and a strictly older write still does not resurrect the record. A 409 on a delete, which means the document moved to a newer version after it was read, is reported as a retryable failure instead of being counted as success; `bulkDeleteByPatient` re-reads such documents at their new version on its next pass and stops when a pass deletes nothing.

## Tests

`ElasticsearchBackendStoreIntegrationTest` (real Elasticsearch 8.13.4 via Testcontainers, `-Pintegration`):

- `bulkDeleteByPatientThenSameVersionRewriteRestoresTheChart` (the reindex contract), `deleteThenSameVersionUpsertRestoresTheDocument` (void then unvoid) and `bulkDeleteThenSameVersionRewriteRestoresTheDocuments` all failed before the change with 0 documents and pass after it.
- `deleteStillBlocksAnOlderRewrite` passes before and after: the conditional-upsert guard survives a delete.

Verification: the integration class runs 37 tests, 36 pass; the one error is the pre-existing `hybridFusesBm25AndKnnViaSpiDefault` zero-vector failure that #89 fixes. The api and omod unit suites build green.

title: Close the ONNX embedding session on context shutdown
body:
Fixes #83.

`querystore.embedding.onnx` now declares `destroy-method="close"`, like the Lucene, Elasticsearch and `SyncExecutor` beans next to it. Before this, Spring never called `OnnxEmbeddingProvider.close()`. On macOS that left each JVM's CoreML-compiled `onnxruntime-*.model.mlmodel(c)` entries in `$TMPDIR`, and the issue has the measurements.

`EmbeddingProviderShutdownTest` (loads the real module context):
- `contextShutdown_closesTheOnnxEmbeddingProvider` runs the context's own destruction callback for the bean and expects `close()` to be called once. It fails without the fix (`expected:<1> but was:<0>`).
- `everyQuerystoreBeanWithACloseMethodIsClosedOnContextShutdown` fails for any querystore bean with a public `close()` that Spring won't call on shutdown. Without the fix it names `querystore.embedding.onnx` and nothing else.

`mvn -pl api verify` passes.

A JVM killed with `kill -9` still leaks, because no shutdown callback runs.

title: The ONNX embedding session is never closed on shutdown, leaking CoreML temp files
body:
The `querystore.embedding.onnx` bean in `moduleApplicationContext.xml` has no `destroy-method`, and `OnnxEmbeddingProvider` is not `AutoCloseable`, so Spring never calls `OnnxEmbeddingProvider.close()` when the context shuts down. The Lucene, Elasticsearch and `SyncExecutor` beans next to it all declare one.

On macOS the session uses the CoreML execution provider, which compiles each CoreML partition into an `onnxruntime-*.model.mlmodel` / `.mlmodelc` entry under `$TMPDIR`. Only closing the session removes them. As a result, every JVM that loads the model leaves them behind: every server start and every test run.

Measured with `OnnxEmbeddingProviderIntegrationTest` (MedEmbed-small, 111 CoreML partitions), counting `onnxruntime-*` entries left in `$TMPDIR` after the JVM exits:

| `@AfterClass` | entries left |
|---|---|
| calls `provider.close()` | 1 |
| skips it | 223 |

On one development machine this had built up to 61,416 entries (about 24 GB) from 497 processes between 2026-09-03 and 2026-10-16, about 7,000 a day during heavy test-server use.

Fix: declare `destroy-method="close"` on the bean, as its siblings do. This does not cover a JVM killed with `kill -9`, since no shutdown callback runs.

title: query cache separator
body:
The separator was a raw NUL byte in the source, which grep and review tools
treat as binary; it is now the escape, byte for byte the same key. The hybrid
SPI test sends a unit query vector, since Elasticsearch rejects a zero vector
for cosine similarity.

title: resolve-ticket 0.29.0, pr-harden 0.41.0, harden 0.44.0, ticket-pool 0.27.0: a run carried past a claude.ai usage limit by CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG
body:
A `/resolve-ticket` run started by hand stalls when a claude.ai usage limit ends its turn. The limit is an API error, which runs `StopFailure` hooks instead of `Stop`, so neither gate sees it, and nothing in the skill runs again until something outside it sends the session a turn. Claude Code's own continue-at-reset can be switched off for an account and skips Remote Control sessions, resets more than a day out and repeated hits in a row; `pool-run` carries only the sessions it starts.

With `CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG` on, a request at the limit waits for the reset inside the turn and retries, so the run never stops. A skill cannot turn that on for the session it runs in, so Step 1 now checks it, and the running Claude Code's version, wherever neither `CLAUDE_PIPELINE_SESSION` nor `CLAUDE_PIPELINE_CARRY` is set (the marks of a session `pool-run` carries itself); when either falls short it says so at once and carries on. The remedy it names is for later sessions, never a mid-run relaunch.

The wait has two consequences this PR also handles. It can hold a live background agent past the gates' one-hour await bound, so pr-harden's State says what such an await gets, and both gates say so when they block past the bound, since nothing in the run's own context marks the hour. And `pool-run` looks for a limit only where a session ends or goes quiet: a headless session waiting under the variable does neither, and a `--work` session waiting on a background agent under it reads as stopped to the carry, which would nudge it beside an agent that had resumed by itself. So the sessions `pool-run` carries start without the variable, and it refuses to start where `~/.claude/settings.json`'s `env` would hand it back.

## Changes

- `resolve-ticket` 0.29.0, Step 1: *Pre-flight the usage limit too*, skipped in a session `pool-run` carries. Step 7's await example records one await per agent.
- `pr-harden` 0.41.0, State: where the watchdog is on, an await past the bound whose agent the harness has not reported is recorded again with the command that recorded it, once; an await names one agent, so a name listed twice is that once spent, and the agent is then stopped (`TaskStop`) before the dead-phase contract retries its phase.
- Both Stop gates (`pr-harden-gate.sh`, `harden-cycle-gate.sh`; hook and skill copies byte-identical): every block reached past the bound opens on the stale awaits, their age and that rule, ahead of the phase's own "spawn a fresh reviewer agent" / "Run Phase 2 once".
- `harden` 0.44.0: the sentence that bounds the await allow points at it.
- `pool-run`: `Session` drops `CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG` and its cap from every headless session, limit probes included; `--work` drops them too while its carry is on (`limit_continue_work`, and `limit_wait_max_seconds` above 0) and marks the session `CLAUDE_PIPELINE_CARRY=work` (with the carry off it pops one inherited), and passes `crossSessionInbound: accept` only then, so a `limit_wait_max_seconds` of 0 no longer opens the session to any local process's messages; `preflight` refuses a watchdog turned on in `~/.claude/settings.json`'s `env` for the driver and a carried `--work`, not for `--claim`, and says to delete the key, since a `0` there overrides the alias.
- `ticket-pool` 0.27.0: `pausing.md` and `by-hand.md` say what carries a hand-started session, what the driver and `--work` drop, and what preflight refuses.
- Tests: both `gate-test.sh` gain an attended stale-await case, a newest-`since` case, a case per block site that the note opens the reason, no-note cases, a case that an unattended yield names its agents, one that an await recorded again is named twice (State's "once" reads that), and, in the pr suite, one that a handover reviewed and verified on its head still ends with a stale await; `pool-test.py` gains three: the environment a headless session's process actually had, a `--work` session's with the carry on, off and at a cap of 0, its launch flag and an inherited marker included, and the settings.json refusal driven through `cmd_work` and `cmd_claim` themselves, for `1`, `" True "`, `yes` and `on`, with the launches and values it leaves alone and the remedy it gives. `test_the_carry_can_be_turned_off`, which could not fail (its stub never served, so nothing could nudge), now refuses once and then serves, checks the switched-off watcher sends nothing and probes nothing, and carries a carry-on control on the same fixture. Each new case was run against the code without the behaviour it pins, and failed; for the gate suites the artifact's `gate-calibrate.py` records which gate mutant each fails against.
- Evidence entries for each rule; budgets in `skill-budgets.json`; the measurements below in `.claude/skill-lessons/artifacts/2026-10-21-retry-watchdog-limit/`.

## The one-time setup it asks for

On Claude Code 2.1.301 or later (the first with the cap):

```bash
alias claude='CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS=18000000 claude'
```

The cap waits out a reset up to five hours away, which covers a five-hour window and refuses a weekly one unless it lands in the week's last five hours. A `pool-run --work` session whose carry is off takes the same two variables in front of that command; with the carry on, the launcher drops them and carries the session itself. Never `~/.claude/settings.json`'s `env`, not even as `0`: it reaches every session `pool-run` starts, and the driver, or `--work` with its carry on, refuses to start under it, while a `0` there overrides the alias.

## Measured against a stub that answers like a claude.ai limit

Claude Code 2.1.306, `claude -p`, an API key and a local stub; `summary.md` has every case with its control.
- Without the variable the first 429 ends the run; with it the request, and a background agent's, waits for the reset and the run finishes. A reset beyond the cap is refused at once, `TRUE` counts as on, and 2.1.42 has no watchdog.
- The turn a limit ends runs `StopFailure` and not `Stop`; a turn that waited ends through `Stop`.
- A waiting background agent is not reported stalled at the default 600 s (an 11-minute wait); at a 20 s stall timeout it is.
- The pr gate allows a yield on a 600 s await and blocks one 7200 s old, opening on the note; recorded again, the await is allowed.
- A headless `pool-run` session waiting under the watchdog streams a retry line every 30 s and no `rate_limit_event`, so the driver cannot suspend it (killed at a 60 s ticket timeout, finished under a 200 s one). With the drop it ends at the first 429, and the `--work` launcher's limit probe answers in 0.8 s, not 305 s. Set in `settings.json`'s `env`, the variable still waits, and a `"0"` there overrode an alias's `=1`: the session ended at the first 429, where with the key absent it waited (2.1.307).
- `pool-run`'s real `watch_hand_launched` nudged a quiet `--work` session once the account, having refused a probe, served one again, whether or not a background agent had been writing its transcript every half second since the first refusal; with no limit it sent nothing. Under the watchdog that nudge would land beside an agent that had resumed by itself.
- The alias, in an interactive bash, starts `claude` with both variables and leaves the shell without them.

Not measured: a real limit under a subscription login, an interactive session, a foreground agent, a wait of hours, zsh.

## Considered and dropped

A skill-armed keepalive: a recurring `CronCreate` job whose prompt resumes the run. A fresh review found it read a run mid-FINISH (`reviewed`, `blocking: 0`) as finished and retired itself while the gate allowed the stop, re-asserted a lifted stop's override, and re-dispatched an agent still running past an hour. In a plain terminal its prompt would also wait behind the usage-limit menu.

## Verification

- `skill-lint.py --against main`: 0 findings, every budget rise recorded.
- `gate-test.sh`: pr-harden 52/52 and harden 56/56 on both copies of each gate.
- `pool-test.py`: 645 passed, 3 failed: the same three that fail on unmodified `main` in this container (two need the installed `~/.claude/pipeline/gate-state`, one macOS `osascript`).
- `/harden`: seven cycles. Cycles 4 to 6 each reopened Phase 1 on a substantive Phase 2 finding: a wait cap of 0 still opening `--work` to any local process's messages, an evidence claim about the gate tests' calibration, the binary's bookkeeping exceptions dropped from another, and a settings test that never wrote `1`. Cycle 6's Phase 1 passes found tests that could not fail, among them `test_the_carry_can_be_turned_off`. Cycle 7's Phase 1 pass and its single Phase 2 found nothing substantive.

After merging, copy `.claude/skills/{resolve-ticket,pr-harden,harden,ticket-pool,skill-retro}/`, `.claude/hooks/{pr-harden-gate.sh,harden-cycle-gate.sh}` and `.claude/pipeline/{pool-run,pool-test.py}` into `~/.claude/` as usual; until the hooks are copied, the registered gates run without the note.

title: Diversify the similarity tier and deepen the default hybrid pools (ADR Decisions 6, 17)
body:
The similarity tier over-fetches and takes records concept by concept,
skipping records a policy tier already claimed, so repeats of one
observation no longer take every slot; repeats are grouped by concept and
rendered value, newest first, keeping each pick's own rank. The default
hybrid pools are deeper, and the Elasticsearch kNN candidate count is capped
at the 10,000 Elasticsearch accepts.

title: Add server-side question interpretation and retrieval preprocessing (ADR Decision 18)
body:
interpret=true on the context slice derives the typed scope and a temporal
flag from the raw question with conservative word-boundary cues, unioned
with the caller's, so a consumer no longer interprets the question itself.
The similarity leg's text is prepared here: lab-panel abbreviations are
expanded and the patient the chart is about is left out, which put the
patient's creatinine records back into a kidney question's slice; every
other word stays for the embedder.

title: Add the tiered context-slice read contract (ADR Decision 17)
body:
mode=context on the patient record read, backed by getContextSlice(patient,
question, request), returns tier-tagged records: a mandatory clinical core,
a recency anchor, typed-complete types, an exact tier and similarity, with
obs-group panel completion. Each page carries chartSnapshotId, sliceId,
effectiveTypes, withheldTypes (requested types the caller holds no core read
privilege for, left out of the scope) and temporalApplied, so a consumer can
tell which snapshot and scope a slice was selected from.

title: Skip records stored at their current version during a bootstrap top-up
body:
A restart's top-up re-projected every record changed since the last
checkpoint while the type stayed RUNNING, 6.4 minutes for 5,000 obs on the
demo data, though steady-state sync had indexed most of them at that version.
BackendStore.findLastModified reports each stored record's version on Lucene,
MySQL and Elasticsearch; a top-up page projects only records not stored or
stored at another version, compared exactly, since core truncates audit dates
to the second. The after-commit pass serializes the saved node again so a
stored version names the committed content, and a condition an edit voided
is deleted and its replacement indexed. A forced resync never skips.

title: Expose patient records over REST with explicit completeness and date semantics
body:
GET /ws/rest/v1/querystore/patientrecord returns the full chart by patient,
or a ranked top-K by patient and q, or q alone. Every mode requires Get
Patients and each record is returned only to a caller holding its type's core
read privilege. Full reads carry a chart snapshot id, chartTruncated and
projectionComplete and support conditional requests; ranked reads fetch one
window at the live maxResultsAbsolute and slice pages from it, so pages
neither repeat nor skip records. A per-patient walk whose page does not end
past its cursor stops instead of looping.

title: Delete Elasticsearch documents at their own version so a same-version rewrite applies
body:
Elasticsearch keeps a tombstone for a deleted document for index.gc_deletes
(60 s by default) and rejects a versioned write at or below the tombstone's
version. Documents are written with version_type=external_gte and
version=last_modified but were deleted without a version, so a per-patient
reindex, a merge sweep or an unvoid that rewrote the same records within a
minute of the delete wrote nothing while reporting success, leaving the
patient's chart empty. Every delete now runs at the document's own version,
a conflict on a delete is a retryable failure, and bulkDeleteByPatient
re-reads such documents at their new version until a pass deletes nothing.
